text: My city should absolutely adopt a carbon price, and honestly I think the only real debate left is over the design, not the principle. A carbon price is a cost applied to carbon pollution to encourage polluters to reduce the amount of greenhouse gas they emit into the atmosphere, and economists across the ideological spectrum broadly regard it as the single most cost-effective instrument for reducing emissions because it harnesses the price mechanism rather than relying on prescriptive command-and-control regulation. What I like about that argument is that it puts the decision in the hands of the people who actually know their own situation. There are two main types of carbon pricing: emissions trading systems and carbon taxes. An emissions trading system caps the total level of greenhouse gas emissions and allows those industries with low emissions to sell their extra allowances to larger emitters, thereby establishing a market price for greenhouse gas emissions. For a single city, though, a straightforward local tax tied to a clear per-ton rate seems way easier to administer than setting up some elaborate permit market that nobody here has the staff to run. We could also send most of the revenue back to residents as a flat rebate, which would keep it from hammering lower-income households. The usual pushback is that prices just rise and ordinary people get squeezed, and I won't pretend that's not a real risk. Critics frequently contend that carbon pricing imposes a regressive burden on low-income households, since energy expenditures represent a larger share of their budgets; however, the empirical literature demonstrates that revenue-recycling mechanisms, such as lump-sum dividends, can fully offset and in many cases reverse this distributional effect. So with a rebate built in from day one, the fairness objection mostly falls apart, and the case for adopting a price here becomes pretty hard to argue against.
